title: The philosophy of curiosity: an exam on the corpus
description: 21 questions whose answers stand in the texts of data/philosophy_corpus. Each reference gives the main point and where it is written, so a person can check every grade. The organism answers from its own notes (its beliefs), not from the books, so a better score means it has learned the point by reading.

questions.question: What does Hobbes call curiosity, and how does he compare its pleasure with bodily pleasure?
questions.reference: Curiosity is the desire to know why and how, found only in humans; Hobbes calls it a 'lust of the mind' whose lasting delight in generating knowledge exceeds the short vehemence of any carnal pleasure.

questions.question: Under what name does Augustine place curiosity, and why does it have that name?
questions.reference: He calls it 'the lust of the eyes', because sight is the sense chiefly used for gaining knowledge, although curiosity uses the other senses too.

questions.question: What does Kant say David Hume did to him?
questions.reference: Hume's suggestion first interrupted Kant's 'dogmatic slumber' and gave his investigations in speculative philosophy a new direction, though Kant did not follow Hume's conclusions.

questions.question: According to Peirce, what causes inquiry, and what is its sole object?
questions.reference: The irritation of doubt causes a struggle to attain a state of belief, which Peirce calls inquiry; its sole object is the settlement of opinion.
questions.source: Peirce, The Fixation of Belief (peirce_chance_love_logic.md, lines 1391-1402)

questions.question: In Plato's Theaetetus, what feeling marks the philosopher, and where does philosophy begin?
questions.reference: Wonder: 'wonder is the feeling of a philosopher, and philosophy begins in wonder' (Iris is the child of Thaumas).

questions.question: What is Meno's objection to inquiry, and how does Socrates answer it?
questions.reference: Meno asks how one can inquire into what one does not know, and how one would recognise it if found; Socrates answers that all inquiry and all learning is recollection.

questions.question: When, according to Dewey, does curiosity become intellectual?
questions.reference: When it rises above the organic and social planes and becomes interest in problems provoked by observation; when the question is not discharged by asking someone else but kept open in one's own mind.
questions.source: Dewey, How We Think, ch. 3 (john_dewey_how_we_think.txt, lines 1188-1194)

questions.question: What happens to curiosity, in Dewey's view, if it is not cultivated at the right moment?
questions.reference: Germinating powers that are not used and cultivated at the right moment tend to be transitory, to die out, or to wane in intensity.
questions.source: Dewey, How We Think, ch. 3 (john_dewey_how_we_think.txt, lines 1196-1197)

questions.question: According to William James, what does the philosophic brain respond to?
questions.reference: An inconsistency or a gap in its knowledge, just as the musical brain responds to a discord in what it hears.
questions.source: James, The Principles of Psychology, vol. 2 (james_principles_psychology_vol2.md, lines 17335-17337)

questions.question: In Hume's section on curiosity, what is the first circumstance that makes truth agreeable?
questions.reference: The genius and capacity employed in its invention and discovery: what is easy and obvious is never valued.
questions.source: Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature, II.3.10 (hume_treatise_human_nature.md, lines 15352-15354)

questions.question: To which pastime does Hume compare philosophy, and what do the two have in common?
questions.reference: Hunting (and also gaming): the pleasure lies in the action of the mind, in attention, difficulty and uncertainty, more than in the end itself.
questions.source: Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature, II.3.10 (hume_treatise_human_nature.md, lines 15425-15444)

questions.question: What kind of scepticism does Hume recommend at the end of the Enquiry concerning Human Understanding?
questions.reference: A mitigated or academical scepticism: excessive Pyrrhonian doubt corrected by common sense and reflection, which also limits inquiry to subjects suited to the narrow capacity of human understanding.

questions.question: Why, according to Russell, should philosophy be studied?
questions.reference: Not for definite answers, which can rarely be known to be true, but for the sake of the questions themselves, which enlarge our conception of what is possible and diminish dogmatic assurance.
questions.source: Russell, The Problems of Philosophy, ch. 15 (russell_problems_of_philosophy.md, lines 3972-3977)

questions.question: What peculiar fate of human reason does Kant describe at the start of the Critique of Pure Reason?
questions.reference: Reason is called upon to consider questions it cannot decline, because they arise from its own nature, but which it cannot answer, because they transcend every faculty of the mind.
questions.source: Kant, Critique of Pure Reason, preface (kant_critique_pure_reason.txt, lines 350-353)

questions.question: What does Pascal say curiosity really is?
questions.reference: 'Curiosity is only vanity': most often we wish to know only in order to talk about it.

questions.question: Which four kinds of idols beset the human mind, according to Bacon?
questions.reference: Idols of the Tribe, Idols of the Den (cave), Idols of the Market (place) and Idols of the Theatre.

questions.question: According to Mill, why must someone who seeks the truth know the arguments against their own view?
questions.reference: He who knows only his own side of the case knows little of that; if he cannot refute the reasons on the other side, he has no ground for preferring his own opinion.

questions.question: What does Confucius say about learning and thought?
questions.reference: Learning without thought is labour lost; thought without learning is perilous.

questions.question: According to Dewey, what are the chief foes of the open-minded attitude in school?
questions.reference: An exorbitant desire for uniformity of procedure and for prompt external results.

questions.question: When, according to William James, may our passional nature decide between opinions?
questions.reference: Whenever the option is genuine and cannot by its nature be decided on intellectual grounds; then our passional nature not only lawfully may but must decide.
questions.source: James, The Will to Believe (william_james_will_to_believe.txt, lines 757-761)

questions.question: What did Descartes resolve to do once in his life, and why?
questions.reference: To cast aside all his former opinions and begin anew from first principles, in order to establish something firm and permanent in the sciences.
